source.title: The gap between theory and practice in function approximation with deep neural networks

record.tranche_reason: The paper varies training sample count and measures generalization error; it explicitly describes double-descent behavior in one experiment, using a function-approximation setup rather than the original study's settings.
record.gate_note: The paper explicitly reports double-descent behavior in its own Figure 18 experiment on a discontinuous halfspace function. It also reports architecture and training results, but those do not establish a fall-rise-fall curve over model size or epochs. The cited double-descent results from other work are not treated as this study's findings.
record.test_reason: In its own Fig. 18 (right), the study sweeps training-sample count for ReLU DNNs fit to a 4-D halfspace indicator function. The authors state the test error shows double-descent behaviour. That is a sample-wise non-monotonicity result in a new setting (regression or function approximation of a discontinuous target). The evidence is a single sentence plus a figure, so it is a weak, incidental test.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Refinement: trained DNNs reach at most about 3-4 digits of accuracy. They underperform compressed-sensing polynomial methods on smooth functions despite strong expressivity results. They do better than CS on less-smooth and discontinuous targets, though their absolute accuracy on piecewise-constant functions is poor and worsens with dimension. A practical existence theorem shows some DNN architecture and training procedure can match CS rates. Double descent is noted only in passing, citing Nakkiran et al.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines function approximation on smooth and piecewise continuous targets using fully connected ReLU networks and sample-count sweeps; it does not reproduce the original study's experimental settings.
record.peer_reviewed: SIAM Journal on Mathematics of Data Science
record.problems: For the reported double-descent result, the curve is available only as a figure and the text gives no numerical values, uncertainty estimate, or peak location. The paper notes that its experiments use one initialization seed, and that broader averaging over seeds is left for future work.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained. Architecture comparisons and training-convergence results elsewhere in the paper do not report a test-error double-descent curve over model size or epochs. Results cited from other work are excluded.

untested.parts: Whether the rise in error with more samples occurs near the interpolation threshold; size of the rise; which architectures show it.
No model-size sweep through an interpolation threshold. Architecture comparisons report only diminishing returns or divergence of large networks, not a second descent.
Test error over epochs is not reported.
Not tested: no capacity sweep past interpolation across model classes.
The noise experiment (App. A.5) does not examine peaks. The regularization (AdamW weight decay) comparison does not concern double descent.

record.verdict_notes: The double-descent remark is one sentence referring to the authors' own figure. It cites Nakkiran et al. §7 (sample-wise non-monotonicity), so linking it to V3 is reasonable. Because the figure values are not in the text, the strength of this support cannot be judged. The study is not an original source. Tranche changed from T2 to T3: the setting is new (scientific function approximation), not a different method aimed at the original question.

versions.untested_parts: The paper varies network architectures and reports architecture-dependent errors, but does not report a model-size fall-rise-fall curve or locate a peak near the training-set interpolation size.
The paper does not measure test error over training epochs as a double-descent curve.
The paper reports double-descent behavior in test error against sample count, but does not identify the interpolation threshold or show that the rise occurs near it.
No general double-descent curve across model classes is tested.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across axes.
The paper includes noise and regularization-related experiments, but does not test whether noise or regularization drives, splits, or removes a double-descent peak.
The paper does not compare the curve against an effective parameter count.

rows.subject: fully-connected ReLU DNNs
rows.size_stated: various architectures; exact sizes not stated for the reported double-descent result
rows.stage_stated: trained; training method for this experiment is not stated in the figure caption
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of training samples and measured average relative L2 test error.

conditions.value: varied; exact plotted values not stated in text

rows.measure: Average relative L2 error; authors describe double-descent behavior.
rows.note: The text explicitly says the right plot shows double-descent behavior. The plotted curve values and the location of any peak are not supplied in the text; the reported result does not establish that the peak is near an interpolation threshold.
rows.check: Training method can be filled in from §3: Adam with exponentially decaying learning rate, single precision, 50,000 epochs or loss 5e-7. Results average 20 trials over data sets, with one initialization seed. The d = 4 sample range runs to roughly 5000 (Fig. 19 right). The text does not say which architectures show the double-descent shape, or whether all do. Nor does it say where the peak sits relative to the interpolation point (number of parameters vs samples). 'Observed' rests only on the authors' wording.

relationships.condition: Fully connected ReLU DNNs, halfspace indicator target (4.4), d = 4, Adam training, sample-count sweep
relationships.reason: Authors state Fig. 18 right shows double-descent behaviour in test error vs samples (r1). Figure-only evidence, and peak location relative to interpolation is not given.
relationships.display_finding: The authors reported double descent in test error as samples increased, without specifying the peak's relation to interpolation.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
